title: Trump and GOP leaders launch an Iowa rescue mission | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Republicans are on a rescue mission in Iowa, touting new plans for a $15 billion steel mill as President Donald Trump and the state’s GOP leaders rush to blunt the political impact of a battered economy and prevent the governor’s office, a Senate seat and three House seats from slipping into Democratic hands in November.

Gov. Kim Reynolds called the Republican-led state legislature into a special session Friday — days afterTrump unveiledthe proposed eastern Iowa steel mill in the Oval Office. After a day of fiery debate, lawmakers overcame fiscal concerns and voted to pave the way for $1.4 billion in tax incentives for the plant near the Mississippi River in Lee County.

Trump’s announcement came the same week the Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s super PAC, announced it was spending another $20 million in Iowa to boost the Senate campaign of US Rep. Ashley Hinson, who polls show is locked in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. The move brings GOP spending in Iowa to more than $100 million.

“For me, it’s always been about going out and earning every vote and running like I’m 10 points behind, which I don’t think I am,” Hinson told CNN on Thursday. She conceded that rising costs are taking a toll, adding: “We do need to bring prices down. We need to figure out how we provide relief to working families.”

The battle Republicans face in Iowa — a state Trump won by 13 percentage points just two years ago — is a window into the party’s broader challenges across the Midwest, where Trump’s war with Iran has sent gas and diesel prices soaring and his trade battles have strained manufacturers’ budgets, increased household costs and limited farmers’ access to foreign markets.

Iowa-based conservative talk radio host Steve Deace sounded the alarm last week,taking to social mediato warn Republicans that “that this might end being an even worse midterm environment than 2006” — the year Democrats gained six Senate seats and 31 House seats to take majorities in both chambers. Deace called the war in Iran a “political albatross.”

“We are risking what’s left of the Trump presidency on this, because if Democrats take control the legislative branch the Trump domestic agenda we all voted for will largely cease,” he said.

Deace urged Republicans to turn attention toward unpopular Democratic positions, while also articulating what victory in Iran would look like.

“The political environment is constantly shifting,” said Johnson County GOP Chairwoman Teresa Bumgartner. “At this point, we have to be focused on the elements that we can control — which is getting our message out.”

The fallout from the steel plant announcement — and the president’s pledge to visit Iowa in the closing month of the campaign to tout the project — has injected a wild card into the final weeks of the midterm election. A promise of creating 1,750 permanent jobs, along with 6,000 temporary construction jobs, comes with a wave of suspicion from Republicans and Democrats alike.

“It sounds too good to be true, and it just might be,” a top Republican official in Iowa told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid agitating the Trump administration.

From talk radio to editorial pages of the state’s newspapers, praise and skepticism of the project has been dominating the political conversation this week in Iowa.

The announcement was met withcomparisons to FoxConn,the Taiwanese electronic giant that fell far short of delivering on plans to spend $10 billion on a Wisconsin plant that would employ 13,000 — a development Trump in 2017 hailed as part of a rebirth of American manufacturing.

“I’m from Wisconsin, home of ‘FoxConn.’ Good luck with your steel mill,” Jason Maloney of Washburn, Wisconsin, wrote in a letter to the editor in the Des Moines Register. “Is a steel mill really coming to landlocked Iowa? People of Iowa, prepare to be grifted.”

Asked whether the project could become an Iowa version of FoxConn, Hinson told CNN: “I don’t think so. I trust our governor who has been working on this deal for months to make sure that we get secure that investment here in Iowa.”

In the Iowa state Senate, five Republicans voted against the measure, saying the $1.4 billion taxpayer-funded tax incentives were fiscally unwise, with a budget shortfall and economic uncertainty looming. The GOP chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, Sen. Dan Dawson of Council Bluffs, was among the critics who voted no.

He said it could be more than a decade before Mesabi Metallics pays Iowa taxes on an incentive package that amounts to about $880,000 for every job created.

“As with anything in life, if you’re not willing to walk away from a deal, you’ll always negotiate against yourself,” Dawson said in a speech on the Senate floor.

While Democrats said they were supportive of the economic development potential, they acknowledged hearing a wave of concern from skeptical Iowans about whether the project was an election-year gambit or something that would actually come to fruition.

Rob Sand, the state auditor who is the Democratic candidate for governor, said he welcomed the creation of jobs, but was reserving judgment until learning more details.

“I want to make sure this is a real opportunity,” Sand, who is facing GOP businessman and farmer Zach Lahn in the race to replace Reynolds, told reporters in Des Moines, “but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced.”

Brad Moudry, who owns a commercial electric business in northern Iowa, said he hoped Iowa lawmakers did their homework on the proposed plant, but said it “sounded good” and could have a trickle-down effect into the broader economy.

“It’s going to take a lot of infrastructure. If they’re going to create 1,600 jobs, is there enough housing for all those people?” said Moudry, a Trump supporter who has been following news of the announcement this week. “It’s going to be a win-win no matter what, but people have to give it a little time.”

The project now is squarely intertwined with the fight for control of Congress, which also runs directly through Iowa. Thefiercely-competitive Senate race, along with three House seats, could play a pivotal role in whether Republicans maintain their narrow majorities in Washington.

Just days after Hinson became the latestRepublican seeking to distanceherself from Trump by calling for an “immediate and successful end to the war in Iran,” she was reeled back in. Standing in the Oval Office a few feet from the president, Hinson praised the steel project, telling the president: “I appreciate your agenda.”

Yet as Hinson campaigned in northeastern Iowa on Thursday, she renewed her call for an end to the Iran war “to provide immediate relief to Iowa families right now,” but she did not mention the steel project. Only when a reporter in Waterloo asked about the project did she briefly mention it, calling the plant “an amazing opportunity for our state.”

Hinson now faces a delicate dance – replicated by many Republicans across the country – of trying to reap the benefits of Trump by motivating his supporters without being carried away by a political undertow of those exhausted by his second term.

Turek is among the Iowa lawmakers who voted Friday to approve tax credits for the proposed steel mill. He said he looked forward to learning more details, saying: “We need jobs more than ever.” But he signaled his intent to keep trying to tie his opponent to policies of the Trump administration.

“Gas and diesel prices have risen more here than almost any other state in the country. We are all paying the price,” Turek said in a new ad released Wednesday. “Ashley Hinson has voted over and over for policies that have jacked up prices, while she gets richer and richer.”

For Iowa Democrats, the last election cycle worth truly celebrating came in 2018 — two years before Caitlin Clark arrived on campus in Iowa City.

That year, the midterm elections of Trump’s first term, Democrats won three US House seats in Iowa — ousting incumbent Republicans in two of them — but narrowly lost the governor’s race to Reynolds.

Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in Iowa since 2008, when former President Barack Obama was on the ballot, the first of two times Obama won the state in a general election.

Not since 1968 has Iowa seen a wide-open race for governor and Senate at the same time, which is one of the factors driving the state’s fiercely competitive election cycle. The decision by two of the state’s top Republicans, Sen. Joni Ernst, and Reynolds, a two-term governor, not to seek third terms has created a rare opening for Democrats.

Yet Democrats still face challenges of their own, including 180,000 fewer registered voters than Republicans.

September voter registration data from the Iowa secretary of state shows that 711,990 voters are registered with the Republican Party, with 529,275 voters registered as Democrats and 564,581 voters not affiliated with either major political party. Independents remain the most important wild card.

Early voting datais offering Iowa Democrats reason for optimism. Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024.

April Melton, the chairwoman of the Black Hawk County GOP, said she thinks Republicans will “buck history” and deliver Trump a strong midterm performance — in part, she said, because she believes the president deserves credit for decisively taking action against Iran without putting American troops on the ground there.

“All we’re doing is paying a little extra in gas,” she said.

But Melton said she sees the midterms much like recent Iowa-versus-Iowa State college football games: razor-tight and likely to be won in the final minutes.

“Fight like you’re losing, always,” Melton said.
